stem: Which DNS server answers this Windows workstation's lookups? Give its host name. (nslookup names the server it asked.)
explain: nslookup fs-01 prints the server it asked: Server: dc-01.office.lan, Address: 192.168.10.5. ipconfig /all lists the same address under DNS Servers. Knowing which resolver a machine uses matters when DNS is filtered, logged or poisoned.

options.text: fs-01.office.lan, the name that was looked up
options.why: That is the name that was looked up, in the answer below.

options.text: gw-01, the default gateway of the network
options.why: The gateway did not answer; the Server line names the resolver.

options.text: ws-win, the PC that ran the lookup
options.why: That is this PC.

options.text: dc-01.office.lan at 192.168.10.5

explain: The Server and Address lines at the top show the resolver asked. The Name and Address lines below are the answer.

stem: What does the Aliases line mean?

options.text: files.office.lan is another name for fs-01.office.lan
files.office.lan is a separate server from fs-01
options.why: The answer is the same host, fs-01.

options.text: fs-01 is down, so the lookup used another server
options.why: An answer was returned with its address.

options.text: The name was found in the hosts file on this PC, not DNS
options.why: The answer came from the DNS server named at the top.

explain: An alias is a CNAME record. The lookup follows it and returns the real name and address.

stem: What kind of lookup is this, and what does it return?

options.text: A forward lookup: the address of dc-01 is 192.168.10.5, found by name
options.why: The query is an address, so it is a reverse lookup.

options.text: A reverse lookup: the name of 192.168.10.5 is dc-01.office.lan
A mail lookup: the mail server responsible for office.lan
options.why: That would need an MX query.

options.text: A failed lookup: the server returned no answer
options.why: A name was returned.

explain: Giving nslookup an IP address asks for its PTR record, mapping an address back to a name.

stem: Which server does nslookup ask by default?

options.text: The default gateway, since routers forward every request
options.why: The gateway forwards packets; it is not necessarily a DNS server.

options.text: The first host that answers a ping on the local network
options.why: nslookup does not search for servers by pinging.

options.text: The DNS server configured on the PC, shown by ipconfig /all
The DHCP server, always, whatever the PC is configured to use
options.why: Only if that is what the PC was configured to use.

explain: nslookup uses the configured resolver unless you name another, as in nslookup fs-01 192.168.10.5.

stem: Both pings below timed out. Is print-01 definitely down?

options.text: Yes, a timeout always means the host is switched off
options.why: Many devices and firewalls drop ping.

options.text: Yes, because the DNS server returned the wrong address
options.why: The name resolved to 192.168.10.40.

options.text: No, because Windows ping never gives a timeout message
options.why: Timeouts are normal when nothing answers.

options.text: No: it may be up but ignoring ICMP echo requests

explain: Request timed out means no echo reply came back. It is a reason to try another probe (a port check), not proof the host is off.

stem: What does TTL=128 in the replies suggest about dc-01?

options.text: Probably a Windows host: 128 is the usual Windows starting TTL
Probably a Linux host, because Linux machines reply with a TTL of 128
options.why: Linux usually starts at 64.

options.text: It is 128 router hops away from this PC across the network
options.why: TTL falls as packets cross routers; 128 is a starting value, not a distance.

options.text: It will stay reachable for the next 128 seconds only
options.why: TTL on a packet is hops, not time.

explain: Different systems start with different TTLs (commonly 64 for Linux, 128 for Windows, 255 for network gear). It is a hint only; it can be changed.

stem: On Windows, which ping option sets the number of echo requests?

options.text: -c count
options.why: -c is the Linux option.

options.text: -n count
-l count
options.why: -l sets the payload size in bytes.

options.text: -w count
options.why: -w is the timeout per reply in milliseconds.

explain: ping -n 4 dc-01 sends four requests. Windows sends four by default; Linux ping runs until stopped.

options.text: Pinging dc-01.office.lan [192.168.10.5] with 32 bytes of data:
options.why: That line only says what is being pinged.

options.text: Reply from 192.168.10.5: bytes=32 time<1ms TTL=128
options.why: That is one reply.

options.text: Packets: Sent = 2, Received = 2, Lost = 0 (0% loss)
Minimum = 0ms, Maximum = 0ms, Average = 0ms
options.why: Those are round-trip times.

explain: The statistics block counts sent, received and lost packets. Loss is the first thing to check when a connection feels unreliable.
